live_web_research.page_text: [2609.39717] Trust Is Not a Score: Runtime Assurance Contracts for High-Risk AI Agents Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2609.39717 (cs) [Submitted on 30 Sep 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 16 Oct 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: Trust Is Not a Score: Runtime Assurance Contracts for High-Risk AI Agents Authors: Serhii Zabolotnii View a PDF of the paper titled Trust Is Not a Score: Runtime Assurance Contracts for High-Risk AI Agents, by Serhii Zabolotnii View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Benchmarks, audits, and agent protocols describe performance, permissions, and repair, but not how observed evidence should change an agent's authority during a consequential task. We propose a Runtime Assurance Contract (RAC), a policy-level formal schema binding autonomy boundaries, component eligibility, evidence state, transition policy, human-review capacity, and non-compensatory gates. Under RAC, soft metrics may inform routing, whereas a failed or unknown mandatory gate forces retry, switch, escalation, deferral, or stop; aggregate performance cannot authorize action. We define the contract, an evidence record, a permission rule, and five invariants. A deterministic failure-injection study in agentic coding evaluates 174 cases, each a distinct mechanism, under a gate conjunction, a score-only rule, and a restricted protocol baseline. At the published example weights and threshold, the score rule admits 56 of 63 block-required injections and all 24 review-required injections; tuned in hindsight, it matches the conjunction case for case. For positive weights, a positive threshold, binary risk signals, and each signal firing alone on some case, the two rules agree on every case if and only if the threshold does not exceed the smallest weight. On 124 further cases written blind by a model of another vendor, the conjunction itself admits 35 of 79 injections, and so does the tuned score rule: a missing detector is invisible to every decision rule. Eighteen hand-authored traces check version-pinned evidence and review transitions. In a prospective synthetic holdout of 24 episodes, RAC and a separately implemented full stateful baseline both match the labels of two blinded LLM judges. These studies test mechanisms on synthetic cases; they establish neither deployed safety nor cross-domain effectiveness. Comments: 18 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. v2 corrects the agentic-coding study (174 distinct mechanisms replace 280 index-cloned cases) and adds an independent 124-case corpus. Ancillary files: decision logs, transition model, LLM holdout. Case files: this https URL (v1.1.0). live_web_research.page_text: Trust Is Not a Score: Runtime Assurance Contracts for High-Risk AI Agents | Arxiv - DeepPaper Trust Is Not a Score: Runtime Assurance Contracts for High-Risk AI Agents PDF DeepRead Key Contributions Proposed the Runtime Assurance Contract (RAC) framework, defined formal invariants for agent authority, and demonstrated through failure-injection studies that gate-based logic outperforms aggregate scoring in high-risk scenarios. Abstract Benchmarks, audits, and agent protocols describe performance, permissions, and repair, but not how observed evidence should change an agent's authority during a consequential task. We call this the assurance-transition gap. We propose a Runtime Assurance Contract (RAC), a policy-level formal schema binding autonomy boundaries, component eligibility, evidence state, transition policy, human-review capacity, and non-compensatory gates. Under RAC, soft metrics may inform routing, whereas a failed or unknown mandatory gate forces retry, switch, escalation, deferral, or stop; aggregate performance cannot authorize action. We define the contract, an evidence record, a permission rule, and five invariants, and illustrate them in clinical, industrial, and judicial failure probes. We then report a deterministic failure-injection study in agentic coding: 280 constructed cases evaluated by a gate conjunction, a score-only rule, and a restricted protocol baseline. At the published example weights and threshold, the score rule admits 80 of 100 block-required injections and all 40 review-required injections. Tuned in hindsight, it matches the conjunction on this corpus. For positive weights, a positive threshold, binary risk signals, zero-signal controls, and an injected case firing each signal alone, we show that exact agreement holds if and only if the threshold does not exceed the smallest weight. A separate set of 18 hand-authored traces checks version-pinned evidence and review transitions against simpler policy variants. In a further prospective synthetic holdout of 24 episodes, two blinded LLM judges assign identical labels to all 72 action attempts; RAC and a separately implemented full stateful baseline both match these labels. These studies test mechanisms on synthetic cases; they establish neither deployed safety nor cross-domain effectiveness. Summary The paper introduces Runtime Assurance Contracts (RAC) to address the 'assurance-transition gap' in high-risk AI agents by replacing aggregate scoring with formal, gate-based decision-making. article.body:
**AI paper proposes runtime contracts to limit high-risk agents**

Serhii Zabolotnii’s paper proposes Runtime Assurance Contracts (RACs), which would tie an AI agent’s authority to evidence and mandatory safety gates. A failed or unknown gate would require the agent to retry, switch, escalate, defer or stop; aggregate scores alone could not authorize action.

In a synthetic coding study, a score-only rule admitted 56 of 63 cases requiring a block. The paper reports no deployment or commercial transaction, and says its studies establish neither deployed safety nor cross-domain effectiveness.
